questions.stem:
A 38-year-old healthy woman comes to clinic 8 days before a trip to rural Guatemala, where she will eat in local homes. She has received all routine childhood vaccines but has never had hepatitis A vaccine. She asks whether it is too late for protection against this fecal-oral infection.

Which plan is most appropriate?
choices: Vaccine now plus immune globulin, then a second dose at 6 to 12 months
Skip the vaccine, since it cannot work in under 2 weeks
Give immune globulin alone and defer the vaccine until she returns home
Give the vaccine now and repeat it every 2 years while traveling
Give the live oral vaccine on days 1, 3, 5 and 7 before she departs the country

explain.html:
Hepatitis A vaccine is recommended for travelers to all developing destinations and should be given more than two weeks before travel. When departure is two weeks away or less, the lecture says to add immune globulin for immediate passive protection while the vaccine response develops.

A second dose at 6 to 12 months completes the series and gives lifelong immunity, so there is no need for repeated boosters. The four-dose live oral schedule belongs to the typhoid vaccine, not hepatitis A.
why: She can still be protected; the lecture adds immune globulin rather than skipping the vaccine.
Deferring the vaccine wastes the chance to start the series that gives lifelong immunity.
Two doses give lifelong immunity; 2-year boosters describe the inactivated typhoid vaccine.
The live oral 4-dose schedule is the typhoid vaccine.
explain.takeaway: Hepatitis A vaccine should be given more than 2 weeks before travel; if 2 weeks or less, add immune globulin, and a second dose at 6 to 12 months gives lifelong immunity.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old man completed the live oral typhoid vaccine (four capsules over a week) before a 3-month trip through South Asia. He tells his travel clinician he plans to eat street food freely and skip water precautions because he is now vaccinated against typhoid.

Which counseling point is most accurate?
choices: The vaccine protects for life, so food precautions are unnecessary
The live vaccine must be followed by the injectable vaccine to work
The vaccine also prevents enterotoxigenic E. coli, so diarrhea risk is low
It is only partly protective, so food and water care is still needed
Freezing ice and adding alcohol to drinks will cover any remaining risk

explain.html:
Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella Typhi, spread by the fecal-oral route. The lecture lists two vaccines: a live oral vaccine (days 1, 3, 5 and 7, finished at least 1 week before travel, boosted at 5 years) and an inactivated injectable vaccine (at least 2 weeks before travel, boosted at 2 years). Both are only 50 to 80% protective, so travelers still need to be careful with food and water.

The vaccine does nothing for travelers' diarrhea from other organisms. The lecture also stresses that freezing does not kill the organisms that cause travelers' diarrhea and alcohol does not sterilize water or ice: "Boil it, cook it, peel it, or forget it."
why: Typhoid vaccines need boosters (5 years oral, 2 years injectable) and are only partly protective.
The two vaccines are alternatives, not a required sequence.
Typhoid vaccine does not protect against ETEC or other causes of travelers' diarrhea.
Freezing does not kill these organisms, and alcohol does not sterilize water or ice.
explain.takeaway: Typhoid vaccines (live oral or inactivated injectable) are only 50 to 80% protective, so careful food and water precautions are still required.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man is planning a pilgrimage to Mecca for the Hajj. He also plans to visit relatives in Niger in February. He received routine vaccines as a child, but none in the past 10 years. The infection of concern spreads through respiratory secretions in crowded close contact and peaks across a band of sub-Saharan Africa during the dry season.

Which vaccine is required for the first part of his trip?
choices: Meningococcal conjugate vaccine (ACWY)
Yellow fever live-attenuated vaccine
Serogroup B meningococcal vaccine
Japanese encephalitis vaccine
Inactivated injectable typhoid vaccine given intramuscularly

explain.html:
The lecture describes meningococcal disease as worldwide but highest in the "meningitis belt" of sub-Saharan Africa, especially in the dry season (December to June), spread by respiratory secretions in close contact. The quadrivalent conjugate vaccine (ACWY) is recommended for travel to the meningitis belt and is required for entry to Saudi Arabia during the Hajj, with a booster after 5 years.

Serogroup B is not a travel-related risk, so the B vaccine is not what travel requires. His February visit to Niger also falls in the meningitis belt dry season, another reason for the ACWY vaccine.
why: Yellow fever vaccine is for endemic areas, not an entry requirement tied to the Hajj.
Serogroup B is not considered a travel-related risk.
Japanese encephalitis vaccine is for certain Asian destinations, not the Hajj.
Typhoid vaccine is considered for many destinations but is not the Hajj requirement.
explain.takeaway: The quadrivalent ACWY conjugate meningococcal vaccine is required for the Hajj and recommended for the sub-Saharan meningitis belt, especially in the dry season.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old woman develops watery, non-bloody diarrhea with cramps on day 6 of a stay at an all-inclusive resort in Mexico. She has 4 to 5 loose stools a day, no fever and is still able to enjoy most activities. Symptoms resolve after 3 days with oral fluids.

Which organism most likely caused her illness?
choices: Shigella species
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli
Giardia lamblia
Enteroaggregative Escherichia coli (EAEC)
Campylobacter jejuni

explain.html:
Travelers' diarrhea is the most common illness in travelers to developing countries, usually starts 4 to 14 days after arrival and is self-limited over 1 to 5 days. Mexico is a high-risk region, and all-inclusive lodging is a listed risk activity.

Bacteria cause more than 90% of cases, and the lecture names enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC, "turista") as the most common offender. Other bacteria (enteroaggregative E. coli, Shigella, Campylobacter, Salmonella), viruses and parasites cause the rest.
why: Shigella is a listed cause but typically causes dysentery with fever and blood, and it is far less common than ETEC.
Giardia is one of the less common parasitic causes and tends to be more prolonged.
EAEC is a listed bacterial cause, but ETEC is named the most common offender.
Campylobacter is a listed bacterial cause but far less common than ETEC.
explain.takeaway: Travelers' diarrhea is mostly bacterial, begins 4 to 14 days after arrival, is self-limited, and is most often caused by enterotoxigenic E. coli.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 35-year-old journalist leaves tomorrow for a 10-day assignment in a region of West Africa with chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum. He wants the prophylaxis option that can start right away and that he can stop soonest after he gets home, because he dislikes taking pills for weeks.

Which regimen best fits his needs?
choices: Chloroquine weekly, starting 1 to 2 weeks before travel
Mefloquine weekly, starting 2 to 3 weeks before and continued 4 weeks after
Atovaquone-proguanil daily, from 1 day before until 7 days after
Doxycycline daily, starting 1 to 2 days before and continued 4 weeks after
No pills, using only DEET and bed nets to prevent mosquito bites

explain.html:
Malaria chemoprophylaxis starts before travel, continues during exposure and continues for a period after leaving. Chloroquine is only for chloroquine-susceptible areas, and mefloquine must start 2 to 3 weeks before travel, so both are out for a traveler leaving tomorrow.

Doxycycline and atovaquone-proguanil can both start 1 to 2 days or 1 day before travel. The difference is the tail: doxycycline continues 4 weeks after the last exposure, while atovaquone-proguanil continues only 7 days. Bite prevention (DEET, nets, staying in screened areas) adds to, but does not replace, chemoprophylaxis.
why: Chloroquine is only for chloroquine-susceptible areas, and it starts 1 to 2 weeks ahead.
Mefloquine must start 2 to 3 weeks before travel and continues 4 weeks after.
Doxycycline can start quickly but continues 4 weeks after the last exposure.
Bite prevention alone is not enough for falciparum malaria exposure.
explain.takeaway: Malaria prophylaxis continues after exposure; atovaquone-proguanil starts 1 day before and stops 7 days after, while doxycycline, chloroquine and mefloquine continue 4 weeks after.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old man returns from Ghana 10 days ago with fever, chills and headache. He did not take prophylaxis. A STAT blood smear shows ring forms inside red cells. He is drowsy and responds only to loud voice.

Hemoglobin: 8.9 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5)
Parasitemia: 7%
Blood pressure: 104/66 mm Hg

Which statement best describes his illness?
choices: Uncomplicated malaria, because his blood pressure is normal
Uncomplicated malaria, because only falciparum causes severe disease
Severe malaria, from parasitemia of 5% or more and altered mentation
Severe malaria only if a repeat smear in 48 hours shows a rising parasite count
Dengue with a false-positive smear, because both cause fever and anemia

explain.html:
The lecture's rule: fever in a traveler returning from a malarious area is malaria until proven otherwise, so order a STAT smear and start therapy promptly. Uncomplicated malaria has parasitemia under 5%, a patient who is not obtunded, can take oral medicines and has no vital organ dysfunction.

Severe or complicated malaria, usually P. falciparum (the likely species after travel to Ghana), includes parasitemia of 5% or more, inability to take oral medicines, impaired consciousness, severe anemia, abnormal bleeding or DIC, or shock. He has parasitemia of 7% and impaired consciousness, and death can occur within hours, so waiting for a repeat smear would be dangerous.
why: Normal blood pressure does not make it uncomplicated when parasitemia and mental status meet severe criteria.
Severe malaria is usually falciparum, which is likely here; that supports severe disease.
Severe malaria can kill within hours, so treatment cannot wait for a repeat smear.
Ring forms in red cells on a smear confirm malaria.
explain.takeaway: Severe malaria (usually falciparum) includes parasitemia of 5% or more, impaired consciousness, inability to take oral medicine, severe anemia, bleeding or DIC, or shock.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 19-year-old college student returns from 6 weeks in Bangladesh, where she ate at roadside stalls. Over the past 10 days her fever has climbed a little higher each day and is now 39.8 C (103.6 F). Heart rate is 78/min. She has diffuse abdominal pain and a few faint, blanching pink macules on the trunk. A malaria smear is negative.

Which test is most likely to identify the cause?
choices: Blood culture
Dengue serology
Stool ova and parasite exam
Urine histoplasma antigen
Zika PCR of urine

explain.html:
Step-wise rising fever, relative bradycardia (a heart rate of 78 with a temperature near 40 C), abdominal pain and rose spots in the second week of illness after travel to South Asia describe typhoid (enteric fever) from Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi. In the first week the fever climbs step-wise with bacteremia; in the third week hepatosplenomegaly, intestinal bleeding and perforation can follow.

The lecture lists diagnosis by blood culture, stool culture and bone marrow culture, with susceptibility testing to guide a fluoroquinolone, cephalosporin or azithromycin. A blood culture is the test that captures the bacteremia.
why: Dengue causes fever with retro-orbital pain and leukopenia, not step-wise fever with relative bradycardia and rose spots.
An ova and parasite exam looks for parasites, not Salmonella Typhi.
Histoplasma antigen tests an endemic mycosis, not a travel-related enteric fever.
Zika causes a mild illness with rash and conjunctivitis, not this course.
explain.takeaway: Typhoid fever presents with step-wise fever and bacteremia, then relative bradycardia, abdominal pain and rose spots, later perforation; diagnose by blood, stool or bone marrow culture.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old woman returns from Colombia with a low-grade fever, an itchy maculopapular rash, pain in the small joints of her hands and feet, and red eyes without discharge. Her symptoms resolve in 5 days. She hopes to become pregnant in the next year.

Which feature of the most likely infection matters most for her plans?
choices: It causes chronic inflammatory arthritis that limits fertility
It can pass to a fetus and cause congenital microcephaly
It can be prevented in a future pregnancy with a live vaccine
It predisposes to hemorrhagic shock on a second infection
It requires a course of antiviral therapy before conception

explain.html:
Low-grade fever, a pruritic maculopapular rash, small-joint arthralgia and nonpurulent conjunctivitis with a mild illness lasting 2 to 7 days is Zika virus, a flavivirus spread by Aedes mosquitoes. The lecture's comparison table shows rash and conjunctivitis are most prominent in Zika, while dengue brings more fever, myalgia and hemorrhage, and chikungunya more arthralgia and inflammatory arthritis.

Zika is neurotropic and spreads maternal-fetal, sexually, by blood products and by transplantation, and congenital microcephaly is its key complication. There is no vaccine; prevention is avoidance, and the lecture advises refraining from unprotected sex after infection (men at least 3 months, women at least 8 weeks).
why: Prolonged inflammatory arthritis is a chikungunya feature, not Zika.
There is no Zika vaccine.
Hemorrhage and shock are dengue features.
There is no antiviral therapy for Zika.
explain.takeaway: Zika (flavivirus) causes mild fever, pruritic rash, small-joint arthralgia and nonpurulent conjunctivitis; it spreads maternal-fetal and sexually and causes congenital microcephaly; there is no vaccine.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 55-year-old woman returns from India with abrupt high fever and severe, symmetric joint pain in her wrists, hands and ankles, with a maculopapular rash. Testing confirms a mosquito-borne virus. Four months later her fever and rash are long gone, but she still has joint pain with prolonged morning stiffness.

Which virus family caused her illness?
choices: Flavivirus, the family that also includes dengue
Picornavirus, a family that also includes hepatitis A
Flavivirus, the family that also includes yellow fever
Bunyavirus, a family spread by ticks and sandflies
Alphavirus, a different family from dengue and Zika

explain.html:
High fever with severe symmetric arthralgia, rash and then persistent arthritis with prolonged morning stiffness for months is chikungunya. The lecture's comparison table gives chikungunya the strongest arthralgia and is the only one of the three with inflammatory arthritis, and persistent arthritis or arthralgia after the acute illness is its hallmark.

Chikungunya is an alphavirus spread by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, which sets it apart from dengue, Zika and yellow fever, all flaviviruses. Treatment is supportive, and vaccines now exist (a live-attenuated and a virus-like particle vaccine).
why: Dengue is a flavivirus, but chikungunya is not.
Hepatitis A is a picornavirus spread fecal-orally, unrelated to chikungunya.
Yellow fever is a flavivirus; chikungunya is not.
Chikungunya is spread by Aedes mosquitoes and is not a bunyavirus.
explain.takeaway: Chikungunya is an Aedes-borne alphavirus whose hallmark is severe arthralgia and persistent inflammatory arthritis lasting months; dengue, Zika and yellow fever are flaviviruses.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A laboratory receives a lung biopsy from a patient with a chronic pneumonia acquired in the Ohio River valley. Cultured at room temperature (25 C), the organism grows as a fluffy mold with hyphae and large spiny spores. Grown at 37 C, the same organism grows as small oval yeasts, the form seen inside the patient's macrophages.

Which statement about this group of fungi is correct?
choices: Infection follows inhalation of the yeast form shed by infected people
Infection usually follows inhaling the mold form from the environment
They grow as molds at body temperature and as yeasts in the soil
They cause disease only in immunocompromised hosts and never reactivate later
They spread from person to person by respiratory droplets in crowds

explain.html:
The endemic mycoses share a pattern: each lives in a specific ecologic niche in the environment and is thermally dimorphic, growing as a mold at 25 to 35 C in the environment and as a yeast (or, for Coccidioides, spherules) at body temperature. Infection follows inhalation of the mold-phase organism, with Sporothrix schenckii as the exception (it enters by inoculation).

Severity depends on the extent of exposure and the host's immune status, hematogenous dissemination is common, and infection can reactivate years later. This organism, a mold with spiny macroconidia and intracellular yeasts from the Ohio River valley, is Histoplasma capsulatum.
why: The yeast form lives in tissue; infection comes from inhaling the environmental mold form.
This reverses dimorphism: mold in the environment, yeast or spherules in the body.
Healthy people are infected too, severity depends on exposure and immunity, and reactivation years later occurs.
These fungi are acquired from the environment, not from other people.
explain.takeaway: Endemic mycoses are thermally dimorphic (mold at 25 to 35 C, yeast or spherules at body temperature) and are acquired by inhaling the environmental mold form, except Sporothrix (inoculation).
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old man from northern Wisconsin who cuts firewood and hunts near rivers has had a cough for 6 weeks despite a course of antibiotics, and now has a raised, crusted, warty skin lesion on his forearm that slowly enlarged. A smear of material scraped from the lesion is examined.

What is the smear most likely to show?
choices: Small oval yeasts packed inside macrophages
Cigar-shaped yeasts with no hyphae in the lesion
Large spherules filled with many small endospores
Large thick-walled yeasts with one broad-based bud
Rope-like hyphae branching at right angles

explain.html:
Blastomyces dermatitidis lives in soil and decaying wood, and its endemic area stretches across the Great Lakes, the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys and the Southeast. It causes pulmonary disease and extrapulmonary disease, with skin lesions a common site of spread, as in this man.

The lecture's images show the tissue form as a large, thick-walled yeast with a broad-based bud. Diagnosis is by fungal smear and culture (with a DNA probe) and antigen detection, more sensitive in urine than serum, and treatment is amphotericin or itraconazole.
why: Small yeasts inside macrophages are the Histoplasma picture.
Cigar-shaped yeasts are the tissue form of Sporothrix.
Spherules with endospores are the tissue form of Coccidioides.
Branching hyphae are a mold pattern, not the yeast form of a dimorphic fungus at body temperature.
explain.takeaway: Blastomyces dermatitidis comes from soil and decaying wood around the Great Lakes and the Ohio and Mississippi valleys, spreads from lung to skin, and appears as large broad-based budding yeasts.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old construction worker who moved from New Jersey to Bakersfield, California, digs foundations in dry, dusty soil. After a windstorm he develops fever, cough and pleuritic chest pain. A lung biopsy is obtained after symptoms persist.

Which finding in the biopsy and which oral drug fit this infection?
choices: Small intracellular yeasts; treat with nafcillin
Gram-negative coccobacilli; treat with doxycycline
Broad-based budding yeasts; treat with metronidazole
Cigar-shaped yeasts; treat with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Spherules filled with endospores; treat with fluconazole

explain.html:
Dusty soil exposure in California's Central Valley (the southwestern deserts are the endemic area) with a pneumonia that will not clear points to coccidioidomycosis. Coccidioides immitis is found in California and C. posadasii outside California. In tissue it forms spherules filled with endospores, rather than a budding yeast.

The lecture lists diagnosis by fungal smear and culture, serology, histopathology and PCR, and treatment with amphotericin and fluconazole (alternatives itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole). Fluconazole is the oral agent the lecture lists alongside amphotericin for this mycosis.
why: Small intracellular yeasts describe Histoplasma, and nafcillin is an antibacterial for MSSA.
No bacterial cause fits this fungal biopsy.
Broad-based budding describes Blastomyces, and metronidazole treats anaerobes and protozoa.
Cigar-shaped yeasts describe Sporothrix, and TMP-SMX is not an antifungal for it.
explain.takeaway: Coccidioides (immitis in California, posadasii elsewhere in the Southwest) forms endospore-filled spherules in tissue and is treated with fluconazole or amphotericin.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 61-year-old avid gardener who works with sphagnum moss and hay pricks her finger. Three weeks later a painless nodule forms at the site and ulcerates, and a second nodule appears higher on the same forearm. She has no cough or fever. Culture of the lesion at room temperature grows a mold with delicate flower-like clusters of spores.

How did she most likely acquire this infection, and what is the treatment?
choices: Inhalation of spores from soil; amphotericin is required for all cases
Mosquito bite; supportive care because no therapy exists
Inhalation of bird droppings; urine antigen guides fluconazole
Inoculation through the skin; itraconazole is a treatment of choice
Ingestion of contaminated produce; azithromycin is preferred

explain.html:
Sporothrix schenckii lives in soil, moss, hay and decaying vegetation, and it is the exception among the endemic mycoses: it is primarily a cutaneous disease after inoculation, not an infection that follows inhalation. Skin nodules after a minor garden injury, with no lung disease, fit that route.

The lecture lists diagnosis by fungal smear and culture, where the tissue form appears as cigar-shaped yeasts and the room-temperature mold shows flower-like spore clusters. Treatment is itraconazole, with amphotericin for more serious disease.
why: Sporothrix is the endemic mycosis acquired by inoculation, not inhalation, and itraconazole is used.
Mosquito-borne illnesses with only supportive care are dengue, chikungunya and Zika.
Bird and bat droppings and urine antigen point to histoplasmosis.
Ingestion and azithromycin fit travelers' diarrhea, not a fungal skin infection.
explain.takeaway: Sporothrix schenckii causes cutaneous and lymphatic nodules after inoculation from soil, moss or hay (the endemic mycosis not acquired by inhalation) and is treated with itraconazole.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 67-year-old man who had his thymus removed for a thymoma 6 years ago is traveling to the Amazon basin of Brazil, an area that requires protection against a mosquito-borne flavivirus that causes hemorrhagic fever and has no antiviral treatment. He has never received the live-attenuated vaccine for it.

Which serious vaccine complication is he at increased risk for, and how does it present?
choices: Guillain-Barre syndrome from direct viral invasion of peripheral nerves
Anaphylaxis that becomes more likely with each booster dose given
Congenital microcephaly in any child conceived within 3 months after the dose
Chronic inflammatory arthritis lasting months after the vaccine
A multisystem illness like natural disease, days after a first dose

explain.html:
The disease is yellow fever, prevented by a live-attenuated vaccine that gives lifelong protection after one dose. The lecture describes yellow fever vaccine-associated viscerotropic disease (YEL-AVD): it mimics natural yellow fever, starts a median of 3 days after vaccination, is fatal in about 65% of cases and has occurred only after a first vaccination, never after a booster. Risk factors are older age and thymus disease or thymectomy, both of which he has.

The vaccine can also cause neurologic disease (YEL-AND), but its Guillain-Barre form is autoimmune, while only the meningoencephalitis comes from direct CNS invasion.
why: Guillain-Barre syndrome after the vaccine is autoimmune, and his risk factors point to viscerotropic disease.
Anaphylaxis is uncommon, and YEL-AVD has not occurred after boosters.
Congenital microcephaly is a Zika virus complication, not a vaccine effect.
Persistent arthritis is a chikungunya feature.
explain.takeaway: Yellow fever vaccine-associated viscerotropic disease mimics yellow fever, follows a first dose by about 3 days, is often fatal, and is more likely with older age and thymus disease or thymectomy.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 31-year-old man backpacking in Southeast Asia develops fever of 38.9 C (102 F), severe abdominal cramps and frequent small stools with visible blood. He is confined to his room and cannot continue traveling. He is drinking oral rehydration solution and asks which antibiotic he should take.

Which choice is preferred for his illness?
choices: Rifaximin
Loperamide alone
Azithromycin
Bismuth subsalicylate alone
No antibiotic, only fluids

explain.html:
Fluids come first for all travelers' diarrhea. Mild disease that does not interfere with activities can be managed with bismuth or antimotility agents. Moderate and severe disease, defined as distressing or incapacitating diarrhea or dysentery with bloody stools, is treated with an antibiotic.

The lecture names azithromycin as preferred for dysentery or febrile diarrhea. Rifaximin and rifamycin should not be used with dysentery or febrile diarrhea, and fluoroquinolones carry adverse effects and resistance concerns, which is especially relevant in Southeast Asia.
why: Rifaximin is not for dysentery or febrile diarrhea.
Antimotility agents alone fit mild diarrhea, not febrile dysentery.
Bismuth alone is for mild diarrhea that does not interfere with activities.
Severe, febrile, bloody diarrhea warrants an antibiotic in addition to fluids.
explain.takeaway: Mild travelers' diarrhea gets fluids plus bismuth or antimotility agents; moderate to severe or dysenteric/febrile diarrhea gets azithromycin, and rifaximin is avoided in dysentery or fever.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 27-year-old man returned from Puerto Rico 5 days ago. He had abrupt fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, myalgias and a rash. Today his fever has broken, and he feels he is getting better, but he now has persistent vomiting, abdominal tenderness and bleeding gums.

White blood cells: 2,600/microL (4,500 to 11,000)
Platelets: 62,000/microL (150,000 to 400,000)
Hematocrit: 51% (41 to 50), up from 44% two days ago

Which statement best describes his current situation?
choices: He is in the convalescent phase and can be discharged with oral fluids
He is in the critical phase, with warning signs of plasma leakage
He needs an antiviral drug started now to prevent severe dengue
He has developed a bacterial superinfection that broke his fever
He has typhoid, since fever that resolves then recurs is step-wise

explain.html:
Abrupt fever with retro-orbital pain, myalgias, rash and leukopenia after travel to the Caribbean fits dengue, a flavivirus spread by Aedes mosquitoes. The lecture describes three phases. The febrile phase lasts 2 to 7 days. The critical phase begins at defervescence and lasts 24 to 48 hours, and patients with significant plasma leakage can progress to severe dengue during it.

His abdominal pain, persistent vomiting and mucosal bleeding are warning signs that predict progression, and a rising hematocrit suggests plasma leakage. Feeling better as the fever breaks is exactly when danger peaks. Treatment is supportive; there is no antiviral therapy.
why: Defervescence starts the critical phase, not convalescence, and his warning signs demand close monitoring.
There is no antiviral therapy for dengue; care is supportive.
Fever resolution here is the natural transition to the critical phase, not a sign of superinfection.
Typhoid has a step-wise rising fever over a week and relative bradycardia, not this pattern.
explain.takeaway: Dengue's critical phase begins at defervescence and lasts 24 to 48 hours; warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding) signal plasma leakage and possible severe dengue; care is supportive.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old man from Kentucky spent a weekend clearing out an old barn where bats and pigeons roosted. Two weeks later he has fever, dry cough and fatigue. Chest imaging shows patchy infiltrates with enlarged hilar nodes. A bronchoscopic biopsy shows macrophages packed with small oval yeasts.

Which noninvasive test is most useful to support this diagnosis?
choices: Urine or serum antigen assay
Serum coccidioidal antibody
Malaria thick and thin smear
Darkfield microscopy of sputum
Stool culture for enteric pathogens

explain.html:
Heavy exposure to bat or bird droppings (guano, a nitrogen-rich soil where the mold phase concentrates) in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, then pneumonia with hilar adenopathy and small yeasts inside macrophages, is histoplasmosis from Histoplasma capsulatum.

The lecture lists diagnosis by fungal culture, antigen assay in serum or urine, and cytology or histopathology, with treatment by amphotericin or itraconazole. The antigen assay is the noninvasive test that supports the diagnosis while cultures grow.
why: Coccidioidal serology targets the southwestern mycosis, not this Ohio valley exposure.
A malaria smear is for a febrile traveler from a malarious area.
Darkfield microscopy looks for spirochetes, not fungi.
Stool culture is for enteric bacterial infection, not a fungal pneumonia.
explain.takeaway: Histoplasma capsulatum concentrates in bird and bat guano in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, appears as small yeasts inside macrophages, and is diagnosed by culture, urine or serum antigen and histopathology.
explain.subject: Microbiology
